warmup.q: A MutableList<Any> holds payment ids. One module adds the Int 1001 by mistake. Much later another module runs val id = ids[0] as String. Where do you first hear about the bug?
options: A compile error on the line that adds 1001
An exception on the line that adds 1001
A ClassCastException on the as String line in the other module
warmup.why: An Int is an Any, so the add compiles and runs. The cast is the only check, and it runs in the reader. The exception names the reader's line, not the line with the bug. A MutableList<String> would have stopped the add at compile time.

sections.h: A cast from Any fails in the wrong place
sections.html:
Before generics, a container that could hold anything held Object in Java and Any in Kotlin. You put a value in, and you cast it back when you took it out. Here is a small settings holder written that way:

Java
class AnyBox { Object value; AnyBox(Object v) { value = v; } }

static void configure(AnyBox box) {
    box.value = 978;                      // bug: the numeric code, not "EUR"
}

static String currencyLabel(AnyBox box) {
    String code = (String) box.value;     // ClassCastException here
    return "Settles in " + code;
}
Kotlin
class AnyBox(var value: Any)

fun configure(box: AnyBox) {
    box.value = 978                   // bug: the numeric code, not "EUR"
}

fun currencyLabel(box: AnyBox): String {
    val code = box.value as String    // ClassCastException here
    return "Settles in $code"
}

The bug is in configure. Someone stored the ISO numeric currency code 978 where the rest of the code expects the letters "EUR". The compiler accepts it, because an Int is an Any. configure returns normally. Nothing fails until currencyLabel runs, maybe hours later, in a class another team owns. The stack trace points at the cast in the reader. The writer is not in it at all.

That is the real cost of Any plus casts. The type check still happens, but it happens late, at run time, and in the wrong place. The error shows up at the read. The bug is at the write.

Generics move the check to the write. Give the box a type parameter and say what it holds:

Java
class Box<T> { T value; Box(T v) { value = v; } }

static void configure(Box<String> box) {
    box.value = 978;                      // now a compile error
}
Kotlin
class Box<T>(var value: T)

fun configure(box: Box<String>) {
    box.value = 978                   // now a compile error
}

Both compilers now reject the bad line itself. javac says incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. kotlinc says:

error: assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String' was expected.

The reader needs no cast any more. box.value is already a String, so currencyLabel cannot throw a ClassCastException.

The compiler messages in this track come from kotlinc 2.4.21. Gradle and IntelliJ print the same text with a capital first letter.

sections.h: A type parameter is a blank the caller fills in
sections.html:
Read class Box<T> as: "Box has one blank in it, called T. Whoever uses Box fills the blank with a real type." T is the type parameter. The real type you put in, like String in Box<String>, is the type argument. Inside the class, T stands for whatever the caller chose. The class never finds out which one.

Java
class Box<T> {
    T value;
    Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
    T replace(T newValue) {
        T old = value;
        value = newValue;
        return old;
    }
}

Box<String> currency = new Box<>("EUR");
Box<Long> limit = new Box<>(50_000L);
currency.replace("USD");      // fine
limit.replace("USD");         // error: String cannot be converted to Long
Kotlin
class Box<T>(var value: T) {
    fun replace(newValue: T): T {
        val old = value
        value = newValue
        return old
    }
}

val currency = Box("EUR")       // Box<String>
val limit = Box(50_000L)        // Box<Long>
currency.replace("USD")         // fine
limit.replace("USD")            // error: actual type is 'String', but 'Long' was expected

One class gives you many types: Box<String>, Box<Long>, Box<Payment>. The compiler checks each one on its own. To the compiler, Box<String> and Box<Long> are as different as String and Long.

How does it check limit.replace("USD")? It substitutes. limit is a Box<Long>, so the compiler reads every T in Box as Long. For that call, replace is replace(newValue: Long): Long, and a String doesn't fit. Fill in the blank, then check the call as if the class had been written for Long all along. Do that in your head and you can predict any call on a generic class before the compiler does.

Functions can have type parameters too. In Java the <T> goes before the return type. In Kotlin it goes right after fun, before the function name:

Java
static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) {
    return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0);
}
Kotlin
fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? =
    if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0]

<T> declares the blank. List<T> and T? use it, and the two uses are tied together. Pass a List<Payment> and you get a Payment? back, with no cast. Pass a List<String> and you get a String?.

A function can have several type parameters, separated by commas: fun <T, K> indexBy(items: List<T>, key: (T) -> K): Map<K, T>. The single-letter names are a habit, not a rule: T for type, E for element, K and V for key and value, R for result.

A method can also have a type parameter that its class does not have. In fun <C> mapSecond(f: (B) -> C): Duo<A, C> on a class Duo<A, B>, A and B belong to the class. C belongs to this one call, and the lambda you pass decides what it is.

One fact to keep for later. At run time there is only one Box class. The <String> part exists for the compiler, and the JVM never sees it. Lesson 8 of this track, on type erasure, shows what that costs you.

sections.h: Inference fills in most type arguments for you
sections.html:
You rarely write type arguments in Kotlin. The compiler works them out from the values you pass. This is type inference, and Java does it too, with var and the diamond.

Java
var amounts = List.of(1200, 350, 99);            // List<Integer>
var box = new Box<>("EUR");                      // Box<String>
var fees = Map.of("EUR", 100, "USD", 250L);      // Map<String, Number & Comparable<...> & ...>
Kotlin
val amounts = listOf(1200, 350, 99)              // List<Int>
val box = Box("EUR")                             // Box<String>
val fees = mapOf("EUR" to 100, "USD" to 250L)    // Map<String, Long>

Look at the last line in each. Kotlin sees 250L in the same map and makes the literal 100 a Long, so both values fit Long. Java never changes a literal's type: 100 stays an Integer, and javac infers a long intersection type for the values instead.

When the values really have different types, the compiler picks the closest type they share:

Java
var mixed = List.of(1, 2.5);     // List<Number & Comparable<...> & Constable & ConstantDesc>
var odd = List.of(1, "a");       // another intersection, of Serializable, Comparable and more
Kotlin
val mixed = listOf(1, 2.5)       // List<Number & Comparable<*>>
val odd = listOf(1, "a")         // List<Comparable<*> & Serializable>

Number & Comparable<*> is an intersection type: something that is both a Number and a Comparable. You cannot write that type in your own code, but the compiler uses it. When you see one, you have usually mixed types by accident.

Sometimes there is nothing to infer from. emptyList() gets no values, so Kotlin has no clue what T should be:

error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.

Java does not complain here. var none = Collections.emptyList(); quietly becomes a List<Object>, which is rarely what you meant. In both languages the fix is the same. Write the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let the compiler work backwards from it:

Java
var none = Collections.<String>emptyList();
List<String> alsoNone = Collections.emptyList();
Kotlin
val none = emptyList<String>()
val alsoNone: List<String> = emptyList()

Each pair means the same thing. I use the first form inside expressions and the second for properties, where the declared type documents the API anyway.

Kotlin builders infer too. buildList { add("idem_1"); add("idem_2") } is a List<String>, worked out from the add calls inside the lambda. Java has no such builder, so there you name the type up front: new ArrayList<String>().

Here is a trick you will use for the rest of this track. When you are not sure what the compiler inferred, assign the value to a type you know is wrong, such as val probe: Int = mixed in Kotlin or int probe = mixed; in Java. The error message prints the real type.

sections.h: Java says the same thing with different punctuation
sections.html:
Java has had generics since Java 5, and Kotlin compiles to the same JVM machinery. The ideas map one to one. Only the punctuation moves.

Java
class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
    T get() { return value; }
}

static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) {
    return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0);
}

Box<String> box = new Box<>("EUR");                    // diamond
List<String> none = Collections.emptyList();           // inferred from the target
List<String> same = Collections.<String>emptyList();   // explicit type argument
Kotlin
class Box<T>(private var value: T) {
    fun get(): T = value
}

fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? =
    if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0]

val box = Box("EUR")                         // no diamond, no new
val none: List<String> = emptyList()         // inferred from the target
val same = emptyList<String>()               // explicit type argument

Three differences matter in practice.

In a Java method, <T> comes before the return type: static <T> T firstOrNull(...). In Kotlin it comes before the function name. The meaning is the same. Java also has no nullable types, so its firstOrNull returns a plain T that may be null, while Kotlin's says T?.

Java needs the diamond <> on new, which tells javac to infer the type argument. Leave it out and new Box("EUR") is a raw type: Box with its generics switched off. Kotlin has no new and no raw types, so Box("EUR") is always a Box<String>.

Java type arguments must be reference types. List<int> is an error (unexpected type, required: reference, found: int), so you write List<Integer>. In Kotlin you write List<Int>, and the compiler stores boxed java.lang.Integer objects for you.

Raw types are why old Java code can still blow up. They exist so that code from before Java 5 keeps compiling. A raw List accepts anything, and javac only warns:

warning: [unchecked] unchecked call to add(E) as a member of the raw type List

The bad value then sits inside a List<String> until someone reads it. Why does the read fail and not the add? At run time the list holds plain Object references, so add(42) has nothing to check against. Where your code reads an element as a String, javac adds a hidden cast to String, and that cast is what throws. Lesson 8 of this track shows that cast in the bytecode. It is the AnyBox failure again, hidden inside a type that claims to be safe. When a Kotlin service gets a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in it, look for a raw type in the Java library underneath.

try.title: Let a raw type smuggle in an Integer
steps: Run RawTypeDemo with the command below. Look for javac's Note: line near the top of the Gradle output.
Predict: does ids.add(42) fail, or does something later fail?

Change the parameter of legacyAppend from List ids to List<String> ids and run it again. Then undo it. (The Kotlin twin has no raw type to remove: it switches the check off with an unchecked cast instead, and fails the same way.)

code.title: RawTypeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A raw type switches the checks off. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out. */ public class RawTypeDemo { // "List" with no <...> is a raw type: javac stops checking what goes in static void legacyAppend(List ids) { ids.add(42); // compiles, with an unchecked warning } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(); // diamond: javac infers ArrayList<String> ids.add("pay_1001"); legacyAppend(ids); System.out.println("size = " + ids.size() + ", nothing failed yet"); try { for (String id : ids) { // javac inserted a (String) cast here System.out.println(id.toUpperCase()); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: RawTypeDemo.kt
alt.html: // Kotlin twin of RawTypeDemo.java. Kotlin has no raw types; the closest way to switch the checks off // is an unchecked cast. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out, exactly as in Java. package workbench.generics.l01.demo // MutableList<*> means "a list of something"; the cast pretends it is a list of anything private fun legacyAppend(ids: MutableList<*>) { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (ids as MutableList<Any?>).add(42) // compiles; without @Suppress Kotlin warns } fun main() { val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // Kotlin infers nothing here: the type is declared ids.add("pay_1001") legacyAppend(ids) println("size = ${ids.size}, nothing failed yet") try { for (id in ids) { // the compiler inserted a cast to String here println(id.uppercase()) } } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } }

try.expect: Gradle prints Note: ... RawTypeDemo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. The program prints size = 2, nothing failed yet and PAY_1001, then a ClassCastException for the Integer. The add worked; the failure comes in the loop, where javac inserted a hidden cast to String. With List<String> ids the build fails at ids.add(42) with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String.

analogy: An Any box is an unlabeled crate in a warehouse. Anyone can put anything in it, and you find out what is inside when you open it at the far end of the building. A Box<String> is a crate with a label, and the loading dock refuses anything that does not match the label. You stop the wrong item at the door instead of at the other end. The analogy breaks in one place: a real label travels with the crate. On the JVM the label is removed after the loading dock, so the check happens at compile time only and the running program cannot read it.
world: Payment services collect untyped bags: a Map<String, Any> of payment metadata, Kafka record headers read as bytes, a JSON blob from the card issuer parsed into a map. Every as String or as Long on a read is a place where a ClassCastException can show up far from the code that wrote the value. When you own the type, give it a type parameter or a real class (data class PaymentMetadata(val merchantId: String, val retries: Int)). When you do not own it, convert once at the edge, in the Kafka deserializer or the HTTP client, so everything behind that line is typed. The Kafka client already does this for you: a ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentEvent> hands you a typed value.
mistake: The common mistake is choosing Any or Map<String, Any> "to keep it flexible" and casting on every read. People do it because it compiles, and the first version has one writer and one reader who agree. Six months later there are five writers, and one of them stores an Int. The fix is to put the type in the signature: a type parameter when the content varies (Box<T>, Cache<V>), or a small typed class when the shape is fixed. If the values really are of several kinds, use a sealed interface, not Any.

compare.title: One generic box and one generic function, in both languages

java.title: Box.java
java.html: import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } // <T> before the return type static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } static void use() { Box<String> box = new Box<>("EUR"); // diamond infers <String> Box raw = new Box("EUR"); // raw type: checks off List<String> none = Collections.<String>emptyList(); List<Integer> ints = List.of(1, 2); // no List<int> } }

kotlin.title: Box.kt
kotlin.html: class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } // <T> before the function name fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] fun use() { val box = Box("EUR") // Box<String>, no diamond needed // there is no raw Box: Box without <...> must be inferable or it does not compile val none = emptyList<String>() val ints: List<Int> = listOf(1, 2) // Int works; stored as java.lang.Integer }

compare.note: The model is the same: one class, type parameters checked at compile time, one runtime class. Kotlin infers the type argument from constructor arguments without a diamond, and it has no raw types, so the unchecked-warning escape hatch that Java keeps for old code does not exist. Kotlin also accepts Int as a type argument, while Java forces you to write Integer. Both compile to boxed objects. One more difference shows in firstOrNull: Kotlin's return type says T?, so callers must handle null. Java's T can be null without saying so.

steps.say: A payment API caches the response for each idempotency key, so a retried request gets the same answer. The first version stores Any, and every caller casts. Find the two places a wrong type could get in or out.
steps.code: class IdempotencyCache { private val responses = HashMap<String, Any>() fun put(key: String, response: Any) { responses[key] = response } fun get(key: String): Any? = responses[key] } // caller val cached = cache.get(key) as AuthorizationResponse? // cast on every read

alt.html: class IdempotencyCache { private final Map<String, Object> responses = new HashMap<>(); void put(String key, Object response) { responses.put(key, response); } Object get(String key) { return responses.get(key); } } // caller AuthorizationResponse cached = (AuthorizationResponse) cache.get(key); // cast on every read

steps.say: 1. Decide what varies. The key is always a String. The response type changes per endpoint: authorizations, refunds, captures. So the response type becomes the type parameter, and the key stays a plain String.
steps.code: class IdempotencyCache<R> { private val responses = HashMap<String, R>() fun put(key: String, response: R) { responses[key] = response } fun get(key: String): R? = responses[key] }

alt.html: class IdempotencyCache<R> { private final Map<String, R> responses = new HashMap<>(); void put(String key, R response) { responses.put(key, response); } R get(String key) { return responses.get(key); } // null when absent }

steps.say: 1. Fill the blank at the use site. Each endpoint gets its own cache with its own type. The cast is gone, and a wrong put is now a compile error.
steps.code: val authCache = IdempotencyCache<AuthorizationResponse>() val cached: AuthorizationResponse? = authCache.get(key) // no cast authCache.put(key, RefundResponse("rf_1")) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'RefundResponse', // but 'AuthorizationResponse' was expected.

alt.html: var authCache = new IdempotencyCache<AuthorizationResponse>(); AuthorizationResponse cached = authCache.get(key); // no cast authCache.put(key, new RefundResponse("rf_1")); // error: incompatible types: RefundResponse cannot be converted to AuthorizationResponse

steps.say: 1. Add a helper that computes on a miss. It uses the class's R, so it needs no <R> of its own. Stop and answer: what would go wrong if you wrote fun <R> getOrPut(...) here? (A new R on the function would hide the class's R, and responses[key] = value would no longer type-check. The same happens in Java with <R> R getOrPut(...).)
steps.code: fun getOrPut(key: String, compute: () -> R): R { responses[key]?.let { return it } val value = compute() responses[key] = value return value }

alt.html: R getOrPut(String key, Supplier<R> compute) { R cached = responses.get(key); if (cached != null) return cached; R value = compute.get(); responses.put(key, value); return value; }

lab.title: Write a generic Stack, two generic functions and a Duo
steps: Run the tests once. All nine fail with NotImplementedError.
In Stack.kt, add a private val items = mutableListOf<T>() and write the five members. pop on an empty stack throws NoSuchElementException.
In Search.kt, write firstMatching with a plain for loop, then indexBy. indexBy keeps the first item it sees for each key.
In Duo.kt, write swap, mapSecond and zipToDuos. Read each return type first: it tells you what to build.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then search your code for as: there should be no casts at all.
hints: For indexBy, a LinkedHashMap<K, T> with putIfAbsent(key(item), item) keeps the first item and the input order.
swap() is one line: Duo(second, first). The compiler checks that it is a Duo<B, A>.
lab.done: All nine tests in GenericsFromZeroTest pass, and your code has no as casts.

drill.title: Write Box and firstOrNull from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In a scratch file, write a Box<T> class with a value and a replace method that returns the old value, plus a generic lastOrNull(items) function. Write it in Kotlin, then in Java. Check: where did each <T> go?

answer.html: class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } fun <T> lastOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[items.size - 1] // Java: the <T> goes before the return type // static <T> T lastOrNull(List<T> items) { // return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(items.size() - 1); // }

alt.title: Box.java
alt.html: class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } // <T> before the return type static <T> T lastOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(items.size() - 1); } }

recap: A cast from Any checks the type late, at the read, so the exception points at the reader and not at the bug.
class Box<T> declares a type parameter. Box<String> fills it with a type argument, and the compiler checks every use.
Kotlin puts a function's <T> before the name (fun <T> f). Java puts it before the return type (static <T> T f).
Inference fills in most type arguments. When there is nothing to infer from, write emptyList<String>() or declare the variable's type.
Assign a value to a wrong type (val probe: Int = x) to make the compiler print what it inferred.
Java raw types (List with no <...>) switch the checks off. Kotlin has none.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to keep a Map<String, Any> of payment settings "because it's flexible". In your own words, explain what a type parameter or a typed class buys you, using where the error shows up.
explain.answer: With Any, the compiler accepts any value on the way in, so a wrong value is only caught by the cast on the way out. That cast runs in whatever code reads the setting, maybe much later, and the exception points there instead of at the code that stored the bad value. With a type parameter, or a small class with typed fields, the compiler checks every write against the declared type. The bad write becomes a compile error on the exact line with the bug, and readers need no casts, so they cannot fail with a ClassCastException. The flexibility of Any is just the freedom to store the wrong thing.

deeper.html:
Two inference tools are worth knowing.

A _ type argument lets you give some type arguments and infer the rest. If a function has two type parameters and only one can be inferred, write _ for the one the compiler can work out: runner.run<CardGateway, _>(). The Kotlin generics page has the full example.

You can also widen a type on purpose. listOf(1, "a") infers an intersection type that you cannot name. If you really want a list of anything, say so: listOf<Any>(1, "a"). Now the type is List<Any> and it reads honestly in code review.

One Java detail: the explicit type argument goes after the dot, Collections.<String>emptyList(), and it needs a receiver. Inside the same class you must write this.<String>helper() or MyClass.<String>helper(). In Java 8 and later you rarely need it, because target typing infers the argument from the variable you assign to.

Finally, Kotlin's List<Int> holds java.lang.Integer objects, so a list of a million ints costs a million small objects. When that matters, use IntArray, which is a real int[].
